key_insight: Visual language models (VLMs) perform well on high-level object recognition but exhibit widespread deficits on standardized neuropsychological tests of low- and mid-level vision, revealing gaps in basic visual processing despite strong semantic ability.
problem_solved: Quantifies and localizes specific visual-processing weaknesses in VLMs by applying standardized neuropsychological tests used for humans, exposing mismatches between human visual competence and model behavior.
method: Administered a battery of standardized neuropsychological visual tests (probing low-, mid-, and high-level vision) to multiple VLMs.
Compared model scores to human normative benchmarks and across test categories to identify systematic deficits.
Analyzed performance patterns by visual processing level and model type to link failures to specific perceptual demands.
impact: Shows that high-level recognition metrics alone can mask fundamental perceptual failures, urging practitioners to adopt richer, neuropsychologically grounded evaluations when building and deploying VLMs. Results guide targeted improvements for robustness and real-world visual reasoning.
visual_elements: Heatmap: tests (rows) × models/humans (columns) showing relative performance and deficits
Grouped bar chart: average scores by processing level (low, mid, high) comparing VLMs vs human norms
Example stimulus panel: side-by-side images of test items with model outputs and highlighted failure modes
Radar chart: per-model profile across key visual abilities (contrast sensitivity, spatial relations, feature integration, object recognition)
paper_title: Visual language models show widespread visual deficits on neuropsychological tests
